newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Rival Cambodian forces clash near ancient temples.
newsitem.headline: Rival Cambodian forces clash near ancient temples.

text.p: Rival Cambodian forces clashed on Friday as fighters loyal to ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh pushed towards Siem Reap town, near the famed Angkor Wat temple complex.

Powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who toppled Ranariddh at the weekend to seize control of the government, sent reinforcements to the area west of Siem Reap, a tourist town 250 km (150 miles) northwest of Phnom Penh.
There had been intermittent clashes in the area over the last few days but more sustained fighting broke out at daybreak on Friday.
"There's still fighting at the same place," a military official said, referring to a location some 30 km (20 miles) west of Siem Reap on the road to Thailand.
"This afternoon the government side sent troops and ammunition from Kompong Cham to confront the other side," said the military official who is loyal to Hun Sen.
"Now the other side is trying to move forward into Siem Reap," he said. He had no word on casualties.
Residents in Siem Reap, home to the 12th century Angkor Wat temple complex, said they could hear shelling. The town, which is under the control of Hun Sen's forces, was quiet but tense, they said.
Japan, meanwhile, ordered three military transport planes to stand by in neighbouring Thailand for a possible evacuation of its citizens as international pressure mounted on Hun Sen.

The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) will try to work out a cease-fire in Cambodia during upcoming talks with warring Cambodian leaders, Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said on Friday.

ASEAN has set up a mission composed of the foreign ministers of the Philippines, Thailand and Indonesia to meet Cambodian head of state King Norodom Sihanouk and the two rival prime ministers to resolve the Cambodian crisis. More than 400 Australians and scores of others were flown out of the country to safety and hundreds of other people queued outside airline offices to join the exodus.
Cambodia's unwieldy coalition government collapsed in violence on Saturday when Hun Sen's forces moved in on Ranariddh's men in the capital. Ranariddh had left the country the previous day.
Hun Sen declared Ranariddh's ouster on Sunday as his forces pushed Ranariddh's men from their bases in and around the city.
Ranariddh on Thursday urged the U.N. Security Council not to recognise any government emerging from the weekend's coup and also called for a freeze in aid to his country.

Ranariddh, speaking to reporters in New York after talks with Security Council President Peter Osvald of Sweden, said he had also asked the council to appeal for mediation in the crisis by his father, King Norodom Sihanouk, now in Beijing.

The international human rights group Amnesty International said in a statement on Thursday there was "compelling evidence of a targeted campaign (by Hun Sen's forces) to eliminate political opponents."

Government officials earlier this week confirmed that one senior Ranariddh loyalist had been arrested by Hun Sen's troops and later shot dead. There were unconfirmed reports of several other Ranariddh men being killed.
Many members of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party have left the country while others remained in hiding in the capital.
But other FUNCINPEC members began moves on Friday to find a replacement for Ranariddh as first prime minister.
Several thousand foreigners have left Cambodia since Phnom Penh's battered airport reopened on Tuesday. Australians, Canadians, New Zealanders and Swedes were among those evacuated on Friday.
The United States announced on Thursday it was suspending its aid programme for Cambodia for at least 30 days in response to Hun Sen's ousting of Ranariddh.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the move was "a clear signal to Hun Sen and his associates that the U.S. will not be conducting business as usual with those individuals."
Germany also said it had suspended its aid programme.
Australia on Friday summoned the Cambodian ambassador to protest at Hun Sen's power grab and warned that aid and military assistance to the country were being reviewed.
